B. During the period of mood disturbance and increased energy and activity, three (or more) of the following symptoms (four if the mood is only irritable) have persisted, represent a noticeable change from usual behavior, and have been present to a significant degree:

1. Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity
2. Decreased need for sleep (eg, feels rested after only 3 hours of sleep)
3. More talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking
4. Flight of idea or subjective experience that thoughts are racing
5. Distractibility (ie, attention too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli), as reported or observed
6. Increase in goal-directed activity (either socially, at work or school, or sexually) or psychomotor agitation
7. Excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful consequences (eg, engaging in unrestrained buying sprees, sexual indiscretions, or foolish business investments)

D. The disturbance in mood and the change in functioning are observable by others

F. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (eg, a drug of abuse, a medication, other treatment) or another medical condition

However, caution is indicated so that one or two symptoms (particularly increased irritability, edginess, or agitation following antidepressant use) are not taken as sufficient for diagnosis of a hypomanic episode, nor necessarily indicative of a bipolar diathesis

A. Five (or more) of the following symptoms have been present during the same 2-week period and represent a change from previous functioning; at least one the symptoms is either (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure
Note: Do not include symptoms that are clearly attributable to another medical condition

1. Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, as indicated by either subjective report (eg, feels sad, empty, hopeless) or observation made by others (eg, appears tearful). (Note: In children and adolescents, can be irritable mood)
2. Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all, or almost all, activities most of the day, nearly every day (as indicated by either subjective account or observation)
3. Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain (eg, a change of more than 5% of body weigh in a month), or decrease or increase in appetite nearly every day. (Note: In children, consider failure to make expected weight gain)
4. Insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day
5. Psychomotor agitation or retardation nearly every day (observable by others, not merely subjective feelings of restlessness or being slowed down)
6. Fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day
7. Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt (which may be delusional) nearly every day (not merely self-reproach or guilt about being sick)
8. Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness, nearly every day (either by subjective account or as observed by others)

C. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition

medical illness, or disability) may include the feelings of intense sadness, rumination about the loss, insomnia, poor appetite, and weight loss noted in Criterion A, which may resemble a depressive episode. This decision inevitably requires the exercise of clinical judgement based on the individual’s history and the cultural norms for the expression of distress in the context of loss

C. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition

document_sections.heading: PURPOSE
document_sections.content: The guideline examines evidence about mental health during pregnancy and postpartum, particularly mood and anxiety disorders, and provides evidence-informed screening and diagnostic guidance. It addresses depression, anxiety and anxiety-related disorders, bipolar disorder, suicidality, and postpartum psychosis. Psychopharmacologic treatment and management are addressed in ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline Number 5.

document_sections.heading: TARGET POPULATION
document_sections.content: The intended population is pregnant or postpartum individuals with mental health conditions. A condition may have begun before pregnancy, first appeared during pregnancy or the first postpartum year, or worsened during that period.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: An a priori protocol guided development. The writing team comprised an obstetrics and gynecology specialist, a maternal–fetal medicine subspecialist, and two external subject experts. ACOG librarians searched Cochrane Library, Cochrane Collaboration Registry of Controlled Trials, EMBASE, PubMed, and MEDLINE. Two writing-team authors assessed studies selected for full-text review against standardized eligibility criteria. Included studies underwent quality assessment, and a modified GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) evidence-to-decision framework informed the recommendations.

document_sections.heading: RECOMMENDATIONS
document_sections.content: The guideline provides screening and diagnostic recommendations for perinatal depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, acute postpartum psychosis, and suicidality. Formal recommendations specify strength and evidence quality. Ungraded Good Practice Points address situations in which inadequate or absent evidence prevents a formal recommendation.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Perinatal mental health conditions affect more than one in five people. They may occur during pregnancy or within the first postpartum year and include conditions predating pregnancy. Despite effective detection and treatment approaches, these conditions often go unrecognized or inadequately treated. Untreated or undertreated illness has harmful short-term and long-term effects that treatment can mitigate, particularly when started early. Reported consequences include impaired mental health and quality of life, reduced engagement with medical care, worsening medical conditions, smoking, substance use disorders, and severe maternal morbidity and mortality. Associated obstetric and offspring outcomes include stillbirth, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction, low birth weight, small for gestational age, impaired bonding, adverse infant neurodevelopment, and later mental health concerns in offspring. Untreated maternal perinatal mental illness is considered an adverse childhood experience (ACE) for offspring; effects can also extend to families, employers, and economic well-being. Severe illness can contribute to preventable maternal and infant deaths. Maternal mortality review committees (MMRCs) identify suicide and overdose or poisoning as the most common causes of pregnancy-associated maternal mortality; the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state MMRCs consider maternal deaths secondary to mental health conditions preventable. Use of validated screening has grown over the past decade, especially for depression, but screening alone is insufficient. Screening should connect patients to detection, assessment, triage and referral, treatment access and initiation, symptom monitoring, and measurement-guided adjustments until remission. Integration of mental health care into obstetric practice has been shown feasible, effective, acceptable, and sustainable; earlier recognition and treatment predict better outcomes. Timely education may help patients and families recognize symptoms. Without an intervention, less than a quarter of individuals whose depression is detected in outpatient perinatal care receive any treatment, defined as an initial mental health visit. Although depression is more common among populations affected by racism and socioeconomic inequities, their screening or treatment rates are lower. The guideline supports obstetrician–gynecologists, midwives, primary care clinicians, and behavioral health professionals. Substance use disorders are outside its scope and are addressed in other ACOG guidance.

document_sections.heading: SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
document_sections.content: The summary groups recommendations for depression and anxiety, bipolar disorder, postpartum psychosis, and suicidality. STRONG recommendations indicate that benefits clearly outweigh harms and burdens, or, for recommendations against an intervention, that harms and burdens clearly outweigh benefits. CONDITIONAL recommendations call for individualized, shared decisions because the balance depends on patient characteristics, values, and preferences. Evidence quality categories are HIGH, MODERATE, LOW, and VERY LOW. GOOD PRACTICE POINTS are ungraded guidance based on expert opinion and available evidence when evidence is extremely limited or absent.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-Based Screening and Diagnostic Approaches to Perinatal Depression and Anxiety Disorders
document_sections.content: ACOG recommends validated, standardized depression and anxiety screening for everyone receiving well-woman, prepregnancy, prenatal, or postpartum care (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE- [DEPRESSION] AND LOW- [ANXIETY] QUALITY EVIDENCE). ACOG recommends screening at the initial prenatal visit, again later in pregnancy, and at postpartum visits (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE- [DEPRESSION] AND LOW- [ANXIETY] QUALITY EVIDENCE). ACOG recommends pairing screening with systems that provide timely assessment and diagnosis, effective treatment, and severity-appropriate monitoring and follow-up (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE-QUALITY EVIDENCE).

document_sections.heading: Evidence-Based Screening and Diagnostic Approaches to Perinatal Bipolar Disorder
document_sections.content: ACOG suggests standardized, validated bipolar disorder screening for everyone receiving prenatal and postpartum care (CONDITIONAL RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE-QUALITY EVIDENCE). Before starting pharmacotherapy for anxiety or depression, ACOG recommends bipolar disorder screening if it has not already occurred (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE-QUALITY EVIDENCE). Because bipolar disorder increases risks of psychosis, suicide, and infanticide or homicide, consultation with a mental health professional, including through Perinatal Psychiatry Access Programs, should be considered for assessment and treatment guidance (GOOD PRACTICE POINT).

document_sections.heading: Evidence-Based Screening and Diagnostic Approaches to Postpartum Psychosis and Perinatal Suicidality
document_sections.content: Following an affirmative answer about self-harm or suicide, ACOG recommends immediate assessment of the likelihood, acuity, and severity of suicide-attempt risk, followed by management tailored to that risk (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, LOW-QUALITY EVIDENCE). ACOG recommends immediate medical attention for postpartum psychosis (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, LOW-QUALITY EVIDENCE).

document_sections.heading: Literature Search
document_sections.content: ACOG librarians searched primary literature in Cochrane Library, Cochrane Collaboration Registry of Controlled Trials, EMBASE, PubMed, and MEDLINE. The initial search covered human studies published in English from 2000 to 2021. Two writing-team members reviewed a November 2022 update using the original systematic process. A final supplemental search in January 2023 sought newly published high-level sources.

document_sections.heading: Study Selection
document_sections.content: ACOG research staff screened titles and abstracts; two writing-team authors assessed full texts against standardized criteria. Eligible studies were in English, included participants identified as female or women, and were conducted in countries ranked very high on the United Nations Human Development Index. Systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and observational studies received priority; case reports, case series, and narrative reviews were considered where evidence was limited. Assessed studies contributed extracted details on design, sample size, interventions, and outcomes to evidence tables.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation and Manuscript Development
document_sections.content: A modified GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) evidence-to-decision framework informed draft statements and their strength and evidence-quality classifications. Ungraded Good Practice Points provide guidance when evidence is extremely limited or nonexistent and draw on expert opinion and available evidence. The Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines–Obstetrics reviewed, revised where appropriate, and affirmed the recommendations and evidence tables. The committee includes a physician triple-boarded in obstetrics and gynecology, psychiatry, and addiction medicine; board-certified psychiatrists reviewed the guideline.

document_sections.heading: Use of Language
document_sections.content: ACOG supports gender diversity in obstetric and gynecologic care. Original guideline text aims to use inclusive or gender-neutral language, while descriptions of research retain the gender terminology used by the investigators.

document_sections.heading: CLINICAL OVERVIEW Mental Health Conditions
document_sections.content: Perinatal mental health conditions encompass illness during pregnancy or the first 12 months after delivery regardless of when it began. DSM-5 generally applies standard diagnostic criteria with a peripartum-onset modifier rather than treating these as distinct diagnoses. The American Psychiatric Association defines postpartum as within 4 weeks of delivery; field experts, including CDC, extend it to 12 months. Depression and anxiety fall within obstetric clinicians’ evaluation and management scope; recognition and initial management of bipolar disorder, postpartum psychosis, and suicidality are also important, preferably with mental health specialist support. Table 1 presents diagnostic criteria for Major Depressive Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Bipolar I Disorder, and Bipolar II Disorder. Depression requires five or more symptoms in the same 2-week period, a change in functioning, and depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure among those symptoms. Anxiety and anxiety-related disorders involve excessive fear or worry and related behavioral and cognitive disturbances. Although DSM-5 distinguishes OCD and trauma- and stressor-related disorders such as PTSD from anxiety disorders, this guideline includes them among anxiety-related disorders. Depression and anxiety-related disorders can involve recurring, unwanted, distressing intrusive thoughts, including thoughts of harm to oneself or an infant; their likelihood of being acted upon must be distinguished. Bipolar disorder, including bipolar I disorder and bipolar II disorder, is usually episodic, often requires lifelong treatment and pharmacotherapy, and may present with depressive, manic, or hypomanic episodes. Because women with bipolar disorder more often present with depressive symptoms, it may be mistaken for unipolar depression. Antidepressant monotherapy in that circumstance can precipitate mania, mixed states, rapid-cycling, or psychosis. Untreated or undertreated bipolar disorder increases postpartum psychosis and suicidality risk. Suicidality includes thoughts, plans, or attempts to take one’s life. Postpartum psychosis is an obstetric and psychiatric emergency that can involve delusions, hallucinations, paranoia, rapidly changing mood, irritability, hyperactivity, sleep disturbance, and thoughts of harming oneself, an infant, or others, with substantial risk of acting on those thoughts. It often occurs with bipolar disorder during depressive, manic, or mixed episodes. Before assigning a mental health diagnosis, clinicians should consider and address medical conditions, substances, and medications that can cause, resemble, or worsen symptoms.

document_sections.heading: Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Perinatal mental health conditions affect more than one in five individuals. Adolescents, military veterans, and people marginalized by racism or socioeconomic disadvantage have higher rates. In a serial cross-sectional analysis of nearly 8 million (n57,906,820) delivery hospitalizations representing almost 40 million (n539,024,974) U.S. deliveries from 2006 to 2015, perinatal mood and anxiety disorders increased from 18.4 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 16.4–20.0) to 40.4 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 39.3– 41.6); severe mental illness increased from 4.2 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 3.9–4.6) to 8.1 per 1,000 deliveries (95% CI 7.9–8.4). Perinatal depression affects approximately one in seven women (14%); onset preceded pregnancy in 27%, occurred during pregnancy in 33%, and occurred postpartum in 40%. Anxiety and anxiety-related disorders appear more likely during pregnancy than postpartum, and perinatal anxiety strongly predicts perinatal depression. Two thirds of women with perinatal depression have one or more other psychiatric disorders; 83% of those comorbid disorders are anxiety disorders, and half of those patients have generalized anxiety disorder. Among women with perinatal anxiety, more than one quarter (28%) also have depression. Across included study populations, specific phobias were reported in 4.8% and PTSD in 1.1%. In longitudinal prenatal studies, 17% screened positive for clinical or subthreshold PTSD; OCD prevalence was 3% prenatally and 7% postpartum, with cumulative incidence of new diagnoses of 9% by 6 months postpartum. Bipolar disorder affects approximately 3% of the general population and 2% to 8% of the perinatal population; one study reported rates as high as 18%. A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated pooled perinatal bipolar disorder prevalence at 2.6% (95% CI 1.2–4.5%) and bipolar-spectrum mood episodes at 20.1% (95% CI 16.0– 24.5%). Bipolar disorder is most often diagnosed at ages 18 to 30 years. For women, the perinatal period carries the highest lifetime risk of first onset and increased vulnerability to recurrence. Overall relapse risk was 37% (95% CI 29–45%); it was 66% (95% CI 57–75%) without pharmacotherapy during pregnancy versus 23% (95% CI 14–37%) when pharmacotherapy continued. For patients with bipolar disorder, psychiatric hospitalization risk is significantly higher postpartum than at other life stages. Postpartum psychosis occurs in approximately 1–2 of 1,000 births and is associated with increased suicide and infanticide risk. Among women with bipolar disorder, reported postpartum psychosis risk is 7–17% or almost one in five deliveries. With prior postpartum psychosis, recurrence was approximately one third (31%, 95% CI 22–42%). A systematic review and meta-analysis of six studies involving 645 patients followed for 11–26 years found that approximately half (43.5%) had isolated postpartum psychosis: 36.1% of the total sample had one episode and 7.1% had recurrence exclusively postpartum. The other 56.7% experienced lifelong psychiatric conditions, including mania, psychosis, or major depression, with psychosis outside the postpartum period. Suicide and substance-use-associated overdose together account for almost a quarter (22.7%) of pregnancy-related deaths; MMRCs considered 100% of deaths due to suicide, overdose, or both preventable. Estimates of suicidal ideation from self-harm items on validated perinatal depression instruments range from 4.6% to 7%. A global systematic review and meta-analysis of 39 articles covering more than 19 million pregnancies reported self-harm prevalence from 0% to 24%. Pregnancy rates across 14 studies and first-postpartum-year rates across 10 studies were both 0–2.4%, with a higher proportion postpartum. Among women with serious mental illness, rates were 0–23.8% in pregnancy across six studies (median 2.2%, interquartile range 0.3–7.9%) and 0–21.9% postpartum across seven studies (median 8.0%, interquartile range 0–18%). In a sequential case series of more than 10,000 postpartum mothers screened for depression, 3.2% reported self-harm thoughts; any self-harm ideation occurred in 19.3% with EPDS scores of 10 or higher and 30% with scores of 13 or higher. Suicidal ideation during pregnancy increased substantially from 2008 to 2018, with the largest proportional increase among Black birthing persons.

document_sections.heading: Etiologies and Risk Factors
document_sections.content: The causes and pathophysiology of perinatal mental health conditions are multifactorial, complex, and usually incompletely understood. Biological, psychosocial, and environmental risk domains overlap, and individuals frequently have multiple concurrent risks.

document_sections.heading: Risk Factors and Correlates of Depression and Anxiety-Related Disorders
document_sections.content: In a stepwise regression model of perinatal depression, race as a social construct, psychological intimate partner violence (IPV), and sexual IPV had the strongest associations. Women with both personal and family histories of depression or anxiety had more than twofold higher antenatal depression risk. Other established risks include previous mental illness or psychiatric treatment, particularly depression or anxiety. Young age, veteran or veteran-dependent status, active-duty service, limited partner support, unemployment, incarceration, insomnia, other sleep difficulties, and high nighttime rumination have been linked to depressive symptoms or diagnoses. More specific correlates of perinatal anxiety, PTSD, or both include pregnancy loss or miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, unplanned or unwanted pregnancy, medical complications including hyperemesis gravidarum, childhood abuse, IPV, sleep disorders, coping styles, personality traits, insufficient social support, prior mental health problems, perceived stress, and adverse life events. Admission of a newborn to neonatal intensive care with low Apgar scores, severe neonatal complications, or both increases maternal depression and PTSD risk. Positive PTSD screening has been associated with younger age, higher parity, a language other than English, more childhood or adolescent trauma, more interpersonal trauma, and more depression and anxiety symptoms. A systematic review of 55 articles associated breastfeeding overall with fewer mental health symptoms, particularly postpartum depression and anxiety; breastfeeding difficulties or a mismatch between expectations and experience were associated with adverse mental health outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Risk Factors and Correlates of Self-Harm and Suicide
document_sections.content: A global systematic review and meta-analysis identified known mental illness, substance misuse, younger age, unmarried status, obstetric or neonatal complications, and previous self-harm or fetal or infant loss as principal correlates of perinatal self-harm. A postpartum major depressive episode, early postpartum depressive symptoms, and stressful events during pregnancy are additional associated factors. A study of pregnancy-associated violent deaths found that homicide decedents were most frequently young, Black, and less educated, whereas suicide decedents were most frequently older and White. Pregnancy-associated suicide risk was 1.6 to 4.5 per 100,000 live births versus 5.3 to 5.5 per 100,000 females aged 10–54 years without a pregnancy. Pregnancy-associated homicide risk was 1.84 times the risk among nonpregnant and postpartum women, whereas pregnancy-associated suicide risk was lower (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.57–0.68). In a prospective randomized controlled trial of 267 women, participants with insomnia and high rumination had 35.6% depression risk and 17.3% suicidal ideation risk, versus 1.2% and 4.9%, respectively, among those sleeping well with low rumination. Perinatal veterans had higher suicidal ideation risk (10%) and history of suicide attempts (30%) than nonveterans. A history of self-harm is an important suicide-risk indicator: one quarter (25%) of women self-harm in the 3 months before suicide, and self-harm accompanying initial severe mental illness predicts later suicide. Suicide mortality is significantly higher with moderate-to-severe mental illness than with no psychiatric history. Among pregnancy-related mental health deaths, three fourths of patients had depression, more than two thirds had past or current substance use, and almost two thirds had Medicaid insurance. Other associated factors include prior suicide attempt, abrupt cessation of psychotropic medication during pregnancy, sleep disturbance, stillbirth, childhood abuse or ACE score 3 or higher or both, financial instability, and major newborn illness. Deaths occur more often in the second half of the first postpartum year.

document_sections.heading: Risk Factors for Postpartum Psychosis
document_sections.content: The leading risk factors are bipolar disorder, personal or family bipolar disorder history, and prior postpartum psychosis. A systematic review and meta-analysis considered Ninety-eight eligible prenatal or perinatal risk or protective factors for psychotic disorders and found significant associations for most; however, most were not amenable to intervention, including parental age, northern-hemisphere birth season, low birth weight, and birth length.

document_sections.heading: Prevention and Anticipatory Guidance
document_sections.content: Prevention is complicated by overlapping biological, environmental, and psychosocial risks. A 2019 U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) report associated counseling, chiefly cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy, with reduced perinatal depression risk (relative risk 0.61, 95% CI 0.47–0.78). The interpersonal therapy–based ROSE (Reach Out, Stay Strong, Essentials for mothers of newborns) program and cognitive behavioral therapy–based Mothers & Babies program lowered depression rates versus controls. Their topics include healthy physical, social, and psychological environments, stress management, support, transition to parenthood, and conflict resolution. Implementation remains difficult despite demonstrated efficacy. USPSTF issued a class B recommendation to offer or refer perinatal individuals at “increased risk” for these interventions but did not define that risk category. Cost-effectiveness analyses in a theoretical pregnant-adolescent cohort supported counseling in that group. In a pilot randomized trial involving women with prior postpartum depression but no antenatal depression, prophylactic sertraline begun on postpartum day 1 after breakfast at 25 mg/day for 4 days, increased to 50 mg/day through week 4, then 75 mg/ day for weeks 5–17, tapered over 3 weeks, and stopped at week 20 reduced recurrence versus placebo (7% sertraline vs 50% placebo recurrence, difference in recurrence rate 0.43, 95% exact CI 20.01 to 0.84, P5.04). Physical activity was associated with lower overall depression scores, but the comparison of groups with and without perinatal depression was not statistically significant. Birth-experience postpartum debriefing and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation were not associated with lower risk. Stopping pharmacotherapy during the perinatal period raises relapse and exacerbation risk; continuation decisions require careful consideration and explicit discussion of untreated-illness risks. Continuation of effective pharmacotherapy for bipolar disorder is highly recommended to prevent relapse and its consequences. Prior bipolar disorder or postpartum psychosis warrants close monitoring, especially in the third trimester and postpartum. When pharmacotherapy was not continued during pregnancy, postpartum initiation of a mood stabilizer can reduce recurrence. Because disturbed sleep may trigger bipolar illness, clinicians can consider planning sleep with support persons or occasionally omitting an overnight feed or milk expression to preserve a longer sleep interval. Comprehensive prenatal intake should cover personal medical and mental health history, obstetric and perinatal mental health history, psychosocial history, family mood and anxiety history, and present and past relevant medications.

document_sections.heading: Health Equity
document_sections.content: People marginalized by racism and socioeconomic disadvantage experience inequities in perinatal mental illness prevalence, screening, treatment, and outcomes. An analysis of PRAMS (Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System) phase 8 2018 data involving 7,328 non-Hispanic Black respondents with live births from 11 states and New York City found higher adjusted depression odds among those distressed by racism in the year before delivery than among those who were not (odds ratio 2.37, 95% CI 1.67–3.37). In a retrospective PHQ-9 screening cohort, non-White women were less likely than White women to receive postpartum screening, and Medicaid or Medicare beneficiaries were less likely than privately insured women to be screened. Barriers to improving depression and anxiety include inequities in access and affordability and comorbid diabetes, obesity, and trauma history. An adjusted retrospective Medicaid claims analysis found that Black and Latina women were less likely to receive depression-related mental health care after delivery and, if care began, less likely to receive follow-up or continued care or refill antidepressants than White women. Treatment rates were inadequate for all low-income women in that study. Evidence about transgender and gender diverse perinatal individuals remains limited, especially for reproductive and perinatal mental health care. Dysphoria, visibility, and isolation may increase risk and warrant further study, monitoring, and intervention when needed. Because no single screening or treatment strategy suits everyone, clinicians are recommended to standardize their approach within their own settings to promote universal access. Collaborative care models may advance equity, although additional perinatal evidence is needed. In a retrospective cohort (N54,710), Black individuals were more likely to be screened but less likely to receive treatment after a positive screen before collaborative care implementation; afterward, screening and treatment following a positive result did not differ significantly between Black and White individuals. Further research is needed on screening instruments acceptable and relatable to people affected by racism and socioeconomic disadvantage.

document_sections.heading: Perinatal Psychiatry Access Programs and Support Lines
document_sections.content: Barriers in obstetric settings include limited mental health training, insufficient standardized workflows, restricted referral networks, some mental health professionals’ reluctance to treat pregnant patients, and limited resources for assessment, treatment, follow-up, and coordination. Perinatal Psychiatry Access Programs aim to strengthen obstetric clinicians’ capacity to care for pregnant, postpartum, lactating, and pregnancy-planning individuals with perinatal mental health or substance use disorders. Services include training and toolkits, real-time psychiatric consultation, community resource and referral connections, and workflow assistance. State and regional programs, national consultation and patient-facing lines, and a U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs Women’s Mental Health Line for VA clinicians are described. The Health Resources & Services Administration offers a free, confidential, multilingual maternal mental health phone or text hotline operating 24/7 at 1-833-943-5746 [1-833-9-HELP4MOMS]. MCPAP for Moms (Massachusetts Child Psychiatry Access Program for Moms), the first statewide program, has been acceptable to obstetrician–gynecologists and has supported evidence-based treatment, including for bipolar disorder. In a CDC-funded cluster randomized controlled trial, MCPAP for Moms participants recruited after positive perinatal depression screening had a clinically significant 4.5-point decrease in EPDS scores.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-Based Screening and Diagnostic Approaches to Perinatal Depression and Anxiety Disorders
document_sections.content: The prevalence, co-occurrence, adverse outcomes, and potential benefits of early intervention underpin widespread support for validated depression and anxiety screening. ACOG recommends standardized, validated screening in well-woman, prepregnancy, prenatal, and postpartum care (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE[DEPRESSION] AND LOW- [ANXIETY] QUALITY EVIDENCE). Positive screening increases the likelihood that obstetric clinicians recommend or provide treatment, particularly under universal screening. Evidence links screening, with or without additional treatment components, to reduced depression risk; it can also reduce stigma and increase awareness and education. Table 2 compares validated perinatal screening instruments, including their item counts, self-administration, test performance, and positive-screen scores. EPDS, PHQ-9, and GAD-7 are commonly used, extensively studied, and validated in multiple languages and perinatal populations. PHQ-9 assesses depressive symptoms and includes a self-harm item; EPDS assesses depressive and anxiety symptoms and also includes a self-harm item. EPDS results were comparable to a structured clinical interview for DSM-5 major depression. A meta-analysis of 35 studies found nearly identical PHQ-9 and EPDS operating characteristics; combined sensitivity and specificity were maximized at scores of 11 or higher for major depression. PHQ-9 and EPDS scores of 10– 14 often correspond to mild symptoms, 15–19 to moderate symptoms, and higher than 19 to severe symptoms and increased bipolar disorder risk. Both are brief, self-administered, and scorable by the care team; patients and professionals have responded favorably. Web-, tablet-, and text message–based screening are acceptable to patients. Anxiety occurs in more than 37% of screened perinatal patients and accompanies depression in at least 28%, supporting screening for both symptom types. The EPDS anxiety subscale uses items 3, 4, and 5, although numbering can vary by layout; a summed score of 5 or higher correlates significantly with a positive GAD-7 screen. If EPDS is not used or a dedicated anxiety instrument is desired, GAD-7 or STAI-6 is recommended in perinatal populations. GAD-7 scores of 5–9 often indicate mild symptoms, 10–14 moderate symptoms, and 15 or higher severe symptoms. ACOG recommends screening at the first prenatal visit, later in pregnancy near or during the third trimester, and at postpartum visits (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE[DEPRESSION] AND LOW- [ANXIETY] QUALITY EVIDENCE). Repeated use of the same validated instrument would ideally identify most symptomatic individuals and create opportunities for anticipatory guidance. ACOG recommends systems ensuring prompt assessment and diagnosis, effective treatment, and severity-based follow-up and monitoring (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE-QUALITY EVIDENCE). Screening scores are not diagnoses: evaluation requires an interview about symptom type, frequency, severity, duration, effect on functioning, recent stressors, and available support, plus consideration of alternative diagnoses. If not already obtained, a positive screen should prompt review of personal and family mental illness, effective and ineffective past psychiatric treatments, psychiatric hospitalization, and prior suicidal ideation or attempts. Clinicians should assess other possible causes, including thyroid dysfunction, severe anemia, and substance use disorder, with symptom assessment and clinically indicated laboratory tests such as thyroid-stimulating hormone, hemoglobin or hematocrit, folate, B12, and iron. Validated substance use screening instruments include 4Ps, NIDA Quick Screen, and CRAFFT for women aged 26 years or younger. All patients warrant counseling about symptoms and potential improvement approaches. Psychotherapy is first-line for depression and anxiety at any severity. Pharmacotherapy alongside psychotherapy is indicated for many patients with moderate or severe symptoms, for those who want medication for mild symptoms, and for those previously requiring medication. Obstetric clinicians should be ready to initiate pharmacotherapy, refer to behavioral health care when indicated, or both; Perinatal Psychiatry Access Programs can assist. After a positive screen, assessment, and diagnosis, serial administration of the instrument can track treatment response and guide titration.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-Based Screening and Diagnostic Approaches to Perinatal Bipolar Disorder
document_sections.content: Bipolar disorder often begins during childbearing years. New and recurrent episodes affect twice as many people in the perinatal period as at other times; conversion from major depressive disorder to bipolar disorder, with first manic or hypomanic symptoms during the perinatal period, particularly postpartum, exceeds 7%. Bipolar disorder can cause depression, hypomania, mania, mixed episodes, psychosis, psychiatric hospitalization, suicide, and infanticide. It is the strongest predictor of postpartum psychosis (1– 2/1,000 perinatal individuals) and infanticide (2–7/100,000 infants). Screening with the other self-administered instruments at the initial obstetric visit could increase recognition; suspected or established bipolar disorder warrants psychiatric referral for further assessment, diagnosis, and longer-term treatment. At minimum, screening must precede pharmacotherapy for depression or anxiety. ACOG suggests validated bipolar screening for everyone receiving prenatal and postpartum care (CONDITIONAL RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE-QUALITY EVIDENCE). MDQ is self-administered and has three questions, the first with 13 items; CIDI bipolar stem is clinician-administered and uses two to three branching questions. MDQ sensitivity ranges from 44% to 90% and specificity from 61% to 92%, depending partly on scoring; detection improves with 7 or more symptoms on question 1 without supplementary functional-impairment questions. CIDI sensitivity ranges from 69% to 100% and specificity from 98% to 99%. Both ask about lifetime experiences rather than the 7 days–2 weeks covered by depression and anxiety instruments. Bipolar screening therefore technically needs to occur only once per perinatal period, though screening with each pregnancy is prudent because onset can occur during childbearing years; a negative result at age 18 years does not predict the result at age 25 years. ACOG recommends screening before initiating anxiety or depression pharmacotherapy if screening has not already occurred (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, MODERATE-QUALITY EVIDENCE). Overlapping depressive symptoms and anxiety-like manic or hypomanic symptoms can obscure bipolar disorder; first-onset nonpsychotic postpartum depression can signal it. Further evaluation identifies bipolar disorder in almost a quarter (22.6%) of people with a positive perinatal depression screen, particularly those with higher depression scores, such as EPDS . 19; conversely, bipolar disorder need not yield a positive depression screen. Antidepressant monotherapy for misdiagnosed unipolar depression is generally contraindicated because it may precipitate mania, mixed states, rapid cycling, or psychosis. A mood stabilizer is generally indicated as the principal pharmacotherapy for bipolar disorder. Table 3 illustrates the CIDI bipolar screen and its branching questions; an affirmative answer to question 3 after question 1 or 2 suggests possible bipolar disorder and may prompt specialist consultation when symptoms are current or other perinatal mood or anxiety pharmacotherapy is contemplated. Given risks of psychosis, suicide, and infanticide or homicide, mental health professional consultation, including through Perinatal Psychiatry Access Programs, should be considered (GOOD PRACTICE POINT). Diagnosis may be complex and delayed for years; suspected cases warrant consultation or referral.

document_sections.heading: Evidence-Based Screening and Diagnostic Approaches to Postpartum Psychosis and Perinatal Suicidality
document_sections.content: ACOG recommends immediate assessment of suicide-attempt likelihood, acuity, and severity after any affirmative self-harm or suicide response, followed by risk-tailored management (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, LOWQUALITY EVIDENCE). Prevention involves screening, assessment, monitoring, and intervention; deterioration more commonly unfolds over time than through abrupt severe symptoms. Anticipatory guidance, follow-up involving partners or support persons, and access to resources can help before a crisis. In a sequential case series of more than 10,000 postpartum mothers screened for depression, approximately 3% reported self-harm thoughts, and suicidal ideation increased with overall depression-screen scores. EPDS question 10 and PHQ-9 question 9 must be reviewed separately from total scores: even a low total score with any response other than “never” or “not at all” requires further assessment. Not every positive response requires emergency services, but every response requires clarification of thought frequency and intensity, intent, plan, likelihood of acting, and whether the contemplated harm is self-injury or intended death. Self-care, support, and treatment participation also inform risk. Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale and Patient Safety Screener can assist non–mental health clinicians in determining whether emergency psychiatric evaluation is needed. Questions about preparations for death, a will or note, access to or acquisition of firearms or poison, accumulated pills, and arrangements for children can clarify imminent risk. Potential protective factors include spiritual beliefs, children, a spouse, and living parents. IPV increases risk: a National Violent Death Reporting System review identified IPV in more than half (54.3%) of mothers who died by suicide; among low-income women in a university clinic, IPV raised antenatal suicidal ideation risk 9.37-fold. Anhedonia and poor self-care are additional high-risk features and can resemble diminished interest in bonding. Outpatient monitoring is appropriate when suicidal thoughts are infrequent, there is no intent, and the person can identify reasons not to attempt suicide. Outpatient options include pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, both, or daytime-intensive partial hospitalization. Concerns about suicidal ideation require assessment beyond screening and an intervention. Whether inpatient or outpatient care is needed, communication with a partner, preferred family member, or another support person is appropriate; they can provide collateral history, help remove potential suicide methods from the home, and receive safety instructions. Patients and supporters should receive resources, with regular reassessment of symptoms and treatment effects. Emergent psychiatric evaluation is warranted with suicidal intent and a plan or inability to explain why an attempt would not proceed; when emergent consultation is warranted, pharmacotherapy and emergent care should begin as soon as possible and continue pending psychiatric assessment. ACOG recommends immediate medical attention for postpartum psychosis (STRONG RECOMMENDATION, LOW-QUALITY EVIDENCE). Postpartum psychosis can be a severe manic, depressive, or mixed episode with psychotic symptoms, or psychosis without a mood episode. Typical onset is 3–10 days after birth; DSM-5 describes onset within the first 4 weeks post-birth, but it can begin later. Presentations include agitation, delusions, disorganized thoughts, bizarre behavior, hallucinations, fluctuating symptoms, and little or no insight, with marked change from usual functioning. Because most cases are new diagnoses and prevalence is 1–2 per 1,000 births, universal postpartum psychosis screening is not recommended. Thorough medical and obstetric history at the first obstetric visit should identify bipolar disorder or previous postpartum psychosis. Patients with previous postpartum psychosis or mania have overall relapse risk of 31% (95% CI 22– 42); with both bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis history, reported rates reach 41-87%. They warrant specialty psychiatric care in pregnancy and postpartum, preferably including a psychiatrist, and a prebirth meeting with the patient, supporters, mental health professionals, and obstetric team to plan pharmacologic prevention, observation, support, and adequate sleep. For those at greatest risk, lithium immediately after delivery has the strongest prevention evidence among the options described. Possible or probable postpartum psychosis requires emergency psychiatric consultation or connection to emergency medical or mental health services, immediate evaluation, admission, treatment, and intensive monitoring to protect patient and infant. The patient must not be left alone or unattended with the infant. Delirium and intoxication with alcohol, benzodiazepines, cocaine, or cannabis can mimic symptoms; substance use assessment should help exclude drug-induced psychosis. After initial safety measures, psychiatric evaluation includes an extensive interview with available partners or family. Inpatient evaluation may include physical examination, head imaging, complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and ammonia; some clinicians also consider lumbar puncture and electroencephalogram. Short-term benzodiazepines or an antipsychotic medication are first-line treatment and can be started by an obstetric clinician while psychiatric consultation is pending. Avoiding overnight breastfeeding may support sleep and early stabilization. With prompt, appropriate treatment, full remission is usually reached by 2 months postpartum. Intrusive thoughts of infant harm can be mistaken for delusions or psychosis. They are common, may arise without mental illness, and are also associated with perinatal depression, anxiety, and OCD. Most women distressed by these unwanted thoughts will not act on them, so infant-harm risk is low, although further inquiry and evaluation are warranted. By contrast, postpartum psychosis requires urgent or emergency recognition and collaboration with inpatient or liaison psychiatry for long-term care.
